description: The chart represents the distribution of problems based on correctness under different settings using Chain of Thought (CoT), categorized by difficulty levels: easy, medium, and hard. Each pie chart is divided into four slices, representing different categories: N+K+, N-K+, N-K-, and N+K-, colored in teal, yellow, orange, and red, respectively. For the "easy" category, the slices are distributed as follows: N+K+ (teal) at 40.6%, N-K+ (yellow) at 45.9%, N-K- (orange) at 10.1%, and N+K- (red) at 3.3%. The "medium" category shows a similar distribution: N+K+ (teal) at 44.6%, N-K+ (yellow) at 44.3%, N-K- (orange) at 7.2%, and N+K- (red) at 3.9%. In contrast, the "hard" category has a different distribution: N+K+ (teal) at 36.2%, N-K+ (yellow) at 36.8%, N-K- (orange) at 20.1%, and N+K- (red) at 7.0%. The chart includes a legend on the right side, and percentage labels are shown inside each slice. The slices are not visually emphasized or exploded, and the categories are not ordered in a particular way across the charts.
caption_used: Problem distribution based on correctness under the w/ knowledge and w/o knowledge settings using CoT. The results indicate that while easier problems are primarily hindered by a lack of knowledge (N−K+ at approximately 50%), medium problems show a consistent dominance of reasoning-based errors (N−K− at 15%). For hard problems, the primary bottleneck lies in the inability to integrate geometric reasoning, as evidenced by the sharp decline in N+K+ to below 10%.
